etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English dich, from Old English dīċ (“trench, moat”) from Proto-Germanic *dīkaz (compare Swedish dike, Icelandic díki, West Frisian dyk (“dam”), Dutch dijk (“dam”), German Teich (“pond”)), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeygʷ- (“to stick, set up”) (compare Latin fīgō (“to affix, fasten”), Lithuanian diegti (“to prick; plant”), dýgsti (“to geminate, grow”)). Doublet of dike.

definitions.definition: A trench; a long, shallow indentation, as for irrigation or drainage.

quote.citation: 2011, Ralph D. Sawyer, Ancient Chinese Warfare‎[1], Basic Books, →ISBN, →LCCN, →OCLC, page 30:
quote.text: Ditches continued to be employed as the sole defensive measure at many sites even after wall building began to emerge. For example, an immense ditch varying between 15 and 20 meters in width and marked by depths of 2.5 to 3.8 meters has recently been discovered in Hubei near Sui-chou.

definitions.definition: (Ireland) A raised bank of earth and the hedgerow on top.

quote.citation: c. 1947, Patrick Kavanagh, “Stony Grey Soil”, Poetry Selections, in Ireland Study Abroad‎[2], University Park, Pennsylvania: Pennsylvania State University, archived from the original on 14 March 2021, page 1:
quote.text: You flung a ditch on my visionOf beauty, love and truth.O stony grey soil of MonaghanYou burgled my bank of youth!

quote.citation: 2013 October 31, Frank McNally, “When Anglophone lines get crossed”, in The Irish Times‎[3], Dublin: Irish Times Trust, archived from the original on 14 March 2021:
quote.text: The original ditches were created by digging trenches, as boundaries and/or irrigation. But to the English, the ditch is the trench. Whereas in Ireland, the ditch is the raised bank of earth and the hedgerow on top. (As for the trench, where I come from that’s a sheugh).

definitions.definition: (transitive, intransitive, aviation) To deliberately crash-land an airplane on water.
(transitive, intransitive) To deliberately not attend classes; to play hookey.

quote.citation: 2005 December 2, Dan Shive, El Goonish Shive (webcomic), Comic for Friday, Dec 2, 2005:
quote.text: "No, instead, it just had enough power to transform me, overload, and force me to wait to change back!  I had to ditch school!"

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From earlier deche, from Middle English dechen, from Old English dēcan (“to smear, plaster, daub”). More at deech.
